terms.gloss: a party; friends eating and drinking together
evidence: Cic. Sen. 45: accubitiōnem epulārem amīcōrum … convīvium nōmināvērunt
terms.comment: A “living together”, as Cicero explains the word (Sen. 45). Traupman’s word for a party: convīvium agitāre, to throw a party (pp. 114, 128; cf. Plaut. Mil. 2.2.10, Lewis & Short: domī agitāre).

terms.gloss: a revel, drinking and merrymaking after dinner
terms.comment: Greek κῶμος: the noisy round of the houses after dinner. Not for a children’s party.

terms.gloss: a gathering, a circle of friends
evidence: Cic. Fin. 5.56: circulōs aliquōs et sessiunculās (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: People gathered to talk, often named beside convīvia (Cic. Balb. 57, Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: frīgoribus partō agricolae plērumque fruuntur mūtuaque inter sē laetī convīvia cūrant. invītat geniālis hiems cūrāsque resolvit
phrases.english: in the cold, farmers mostly enjoy what they have earned, and happily give parties for one another; festive winter invites them and loosens their cares
I’m going to throw a party for him.

sources: Lewis & Short: convivium · Lewis & Short: comissatio · Lewis & Short: circulus
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 114, 128, checked against the searchable text of the book (9 November 2026).
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. party (subst.), get-together (social gathering).
Cicero and Vergil from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-cicero-philosophica, loci-vergilius).
